## BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA

Joshua Lanclos/APEA

## Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia

- Noncancerous enlargement of the prostate gland
- 80% of men have BPH by the age of 80.

## QUESTION #1

A 65-year-old male patient presents with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS). Which of the following is not a common finding in a patient diagnosed with BPH?

1. Nocturia
2. Postvoid dribbling
3. Hematuria
4. Weak urinary stream

## BPH: Assessment Findings

## LOWER URINARY TRACT SYMPTOMS (LUTS)

- Change in urine stream: force, caliber, splitting
- Hesitancy, postvoid dribbling
- Incontinence
- Frequency, urgency, nocturia
- Incomplete bladder emptying, retention

## OBJECTIVE FINDINGS

- Firm, smooth, symmetrically enlarged prostate
- Elevated PSA

<!-- image -->

## Enlarged Prostate

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #2

Which of the following is a potential complication of untreated BPH?

1. Prostate cancer
2. Rhabdomyolysis
3. Varicocele
4. Recurrent urinary tract infections

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #3

A patient has a new diagnosis of BPH. Which of the following statements is true?

1. BPH medications work by blocking alpha receptors in the prostate.
2. Alpha-adrenergic antagonists (e.g., doxazosin) are rarely used to treat BPH.
3. A baseline PSA level is not necessary prior to the initiation of a 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (5ARIs).
4. Using alpha blockers and 5-ARIs concurrently to treat BPH is contraindicated.

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES BPH: Management

Alpha receptors are abundant in prostate, base of bladder, prostate capsule, and prostatic urethra.

| Alpha-adrenergic antagonists: decrease bladder outlet obstruction                   |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| · Terazosin, tamsulosin, doxazosin                                                  |
| 5-alpha reductase inhibitors: reduce the size of the prostate                       |
| · 6-12 months of treatment necessary to see full benefit · Dutasteride, finasteride |
| PDE-5 inhibitor: relax bladder outlet and prostate smooth muscle                    |
| · Tadalafil                                                                         |

Combo (Jalyn) = dutasteride + tamsulosin

## Alpha Blockers Education and Precautions

Caution with orthostatic hypotension

Selective alpha blockers were originally used for blood pressure management.

| Uroselective                | Comments                                                               |
|-----------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Alfuzosin/Uroxatral         | Alfuzosin (needs renal and hepatic dose adjustments)                   |
| Tamsulosin/Flomax (generic) | Tamsulosin (no renal or hepatic precautions); sulfa allergy precaution |
| Silodosin/Rapaflo           | Silodosin (needs renal and hepatic dose adjustments)                   |

## QUESTION #4

A differential diagnosis is created for a 70-year-old male patient who has lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS). Which of the following disorders is least likely to cause these symptoms?

1. Prostate cancer
2. Prostatitis
3. Urinary tract infection
4. Benign prostatic hypertrophy

## PROSTATE CANCER

- Malignancy of the prostate gland
- Most common cancer in men
- Lifetime risk is 16%
- Risk of dying from prostate cancer is 2.9%.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Prostate Cancer Risk Factors

- Older age
- Black men
- Family history of prostate cancer
- $ First-degree relative
- $ <65 years
- Known or likely BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene mutations

Men who have risk factors profit most from screening!

## Factors Affecting PSA

Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is a protein produced by the prostate gland when it is active.

| Activities and their impact on PSA levels - No Change   | Activities and their impact on PSA levels   | Activities and their impact on PSA levels   |
|---------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| Bed rest                                                | Ejaculation (within 24 hours)               | 5-ARIs (order PSA prior to initiation)      |
| Exercise                                                | DRE (clinically insignificant)              |                                             |
|                                                         | Cycling                                     |                                             |
|                                                         | Prostate infection                          |                                             |
|                                                         | Prostate massage                            |                                             |

## Prostate Cancer Assessment

- History
- $ Most patients are asymptomatic at diagnosis.
- $ May have new-onset ED and/or obstructive symptoms.
- Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
- $ Sensitivity 21%; specificity 91%
- $ PSA >4 is suspicious.
- $ PSA value does not rule out/rule in prostate cancer.
- Digital rectal exam (DRE)
- $ Asymmetry, induration, nodularity are suspicious of prostate cancer even if normal PSA.

## QUESTION #5

Which of the following patients does NOT warrant a referral to Urology?

1. A 48-year-old who has nodules and induration on DRE, PSA of 3.5 ng/mL
2. A 55-year-old taking finasteride for BPH, PSA 2.8 ng/mL and now 3.3 ng/mL
3. A 45-year-old who reports ED and has a PSA of 4.4 ng/mL
4. A 60-year-old who has acute prostatitis and a PSA of 6.0 ng/mL

<!-- image -->

## Prostate Cancer Screening Principles

- Risk-based assessment: age 40
- Screen with PSA: age 50-55, every 1-2 years
- Shared decision-making (risk vs. benefits)
- $ Screen if at least 10 years of longevity
- $ Usually stop screening at age 70-75 years
- Digital rectal examination (DRE) no longer recommended for screening

Remember: Screening is for asymptomatic patients!

## QUESTION #6

A 45-year-old male patient reports fever, dysuria, bilateral pelvic pain, and pain with morning bowel movement. Which of the following is the most likely differential diagnosis?

1. Uncomplicated urinary tract infection
2. Nephrolithiasis
3. Pyelonephritis
4. Acute bacterial prostatitis

## ACUTE BACTERIAL PROSTATITIS

## Acute Bacterial Prostatitis (ABP)

- Infection/inflammation of prostate
- $ Usually caused by ascending infection from urethritis, cystitis, and epididymitis
- Etiology
- $ Gram-negative organisms: E. coli, Proteus sp.
- $ STIs: C. trachomatis, Ureaplasma, T. vaginalis

## Acute Bacterial Prostatitis: History

- Acute pain: perineum, lower abdomen, testicles, or tip of the penis
- Pain with ejaculation and/or defecation
- Voiding difficulty: frequency, urgency, dysuria, nocturia
- Acutely ill: fever, chills, malaise, myalgias

## Acute Bacterial Prostatitis: Assessment

- Digital rectal exam
- $ Enlarged, firm or boggy, EXQUISITELY tender prostate
- $ Avoid vigorous massage.
- $ Assess for CVA tenderness.
- Urinalysis/urine culture:
- $ Hematuria
- $ Cloudy
- $ Pyuria/bacteriuria
- $ Leukocytosis
- STI testing if at risk
- PSA will be elevated

<!-- image -->

© leonello calvetti/Shutterstock, Inc

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Management: Acute Bacterial Prostatitis

- Antibiotics for 2-6 weeks (empiric pending C&S)
- $ No STI risk:
- Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, or TMP-SMX
- $ STI risk: (gonorrhea/chlamydia)
- 1g ceftriaxone (Rocephin) PLUS 2 weeks of doxycycline
- Expected course
- $ Symptoms improve in 2-6 days.
- $ Negative urinalysis at 7 days predicts cure IF patient completes full course of antibiotics.
- Defer PSA screening for 1 month after treatment.

## Chronic Bacterial Prostatitis

- Cause: often untreated or undertreated acute prostatitis
- Symptoms: usually subtle, variable urologic pain, frequency, urgency
- Prostate exam is usually normal.
- Empiric antibiotics: 4-6 weeks
- Obtain urine culture.
- Possible NSAIDs, alpha blocker

Maintain a LOW threshold for UROLOGY referral!!!

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES

## MALE SEXUAL WELLNESS CONCERNS

- Diminished libido
- $ Comorbid sexual and voiding disorders
- Ejaculatory disorders
- $ Premature
- $ Delayed
- $ Retrograde
- $ Anorgasmia
- Erectile dysfunction
- $ Acquire or sustain an erection
- $ Lack of sufficient rigidity
- $ Duration for sexual intercourse

Obtain a good sexual history!

## QUESTION #7

Which of the following is NOT a risk factor for erectile dysfunction?

1. Cardiovascular disease
2. Neurologic issues
3. History of gonorrhea
4. Use of antidepressants

## Erectile Dysfunction (ED)

| Physiologic causes                                                                                                                                                                        | Psychogenic causes                                                                                                |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| · Medications · Microvascular conditions · Neurologic disorders · Obstructive sleep apnea · Chronic kidney disease · Drug use disorder · Smoking · Hypo/hyperthyroidism · Prostate cancer | · Depression · Stress · Relationship issues If nocturnal erection is present, consider a psychogenic cause of ED. |

## Medical Evaluation of ED

- History and physical exam
- $ 95% sensitive
- $ 50% specific
- Referral for nocturnal penile tumescence testing
- Duplex Doppler imaging
- CBC, TSH
- PSA
- Hormone levels

<!-- image -->

## Low Testosterone

Suspect low testosterone (T) based on these signs and symptoms.

| Sexual                    | Physical                 | Cognitive             |
|---------------------------|--------------------------|-----------------------|
| Reduced sexual drive      | Fatigue                  | Depression            |
| Reduced erectile function | Hair loss                | Cognitive dysfunction |
|                           | Reduced lean muscle mass | Irritability          |
|                           | Obesity                  |                       |
|                           | Gynecomastia             |                       |

Testosterone therapy improves:

- Sexual function and libido
- Muscle mass
- Mood
- Anemia
- Insulin sensitivity
- Bone density

Low T: Less Than 300 ng/dL

<!-- image -->

NOTES

## NOTES PDE5 Inhibitors

Primarily used to treat ED & LUTS

- Viagra (sildenafil)
- Stendra (avanafil)
- $ Fastest acting
- Cialis (tadalafil)
- $ Also useful in BPH, longest-acting
- Levitra, Staxyn (vardenafil)

Cautious use: CVD

Contraindicated: nitrates

## QUESTION #8

A patient presents with ED and desires to start a PDE5 Inhibitor. Which of the following is an absolute contraindication?

1. Losartan
2. Isosorbide
3. Tamsulosin
4. Dapagliflozin

## COMMON CONCERNS

## QUESTION #9

A 36-year-old male bus driver who reports testicular pain and swelling is examined. Symptoms began yesterday after a 12-hour shift and have gradually increased. What diagnosis is suspected?

1. Acute bacterial prostatitis
2. Prostate cancer
3. Chronic prostatitis
4. Epididymitis

## Acute Scrotal Pain

| Disorder                | Symptom Onset    | Cremasteric Reflex                      | Prehn Sign                              | Comments                                                            |
|-------------------------|------------------|-----------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Epididymitis (orchitis) | Acute or chronic | Positive (testicle will rise-normal)    | Positive (pain resolves with elevation) | · Tenderness of epididymis · If STI, positive culture or urethritis |
| Testicular torsion      | Acute            | Negative (testicle WON'T rise-abnormal) | Negative (pain remains with elevation)  | · Urologic emergency · Testicular swelling, high-riding testicle    |

<!-- image -->

## EPIDIDYMITIS

## Epididymitis: Etiology

- Noninfectious causes: most common
- $ Reflux of urine through the ejaculatory ducts and vas deferens into epididymis
- $ Prolonged sitting
- $ Underlying congenital defect
- Infectious: rare unless STI
- $ 75% of time: C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae
- $ C. trachomatis most common

## Epididymitis: Clinical Presentation

- Gradual development of scrotal pain
- Dysuria
- Physical exam
- $ Epididymis very tender, enlarged, and indurated
- $ May have urethral discharge if gonorrhea
- $ Positive Prehn sign: relief of pain with scrotal elevation

<!-- image -->

## Epididymitis: Diagnostic Studies

- Urinalysis + culture
- $ Normal in noninfectious epididymitis
- $ Pyuria: think infectious!
- NAAT for C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae
- Ultrasound if no improvement or an uncertain diagnosis

## Epididymitis: Management

- Noninfectious, no severe pain
- $ Treatment is conservative: rest, oral fluids, scrotal support, ice.
- $ NSAIDs/analgesics
- Infectious (based on culture)
- $ Gonorrhea: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM
- $ Chlamydia: doxycycline 100 mg BID ×10 days

Expect improvement within 3 days.

Full resolution within 2-4 weeks of treatment Joshua Lanclos/APEA

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #10

A 19-year-old male has severe groin pain, nausea, and vomiting. He was kneed in the groin during football 3 hours ago. On examination, the right testicle is very tender, hard, and swollen with a negative cremasteric reflex. Which action should be taken?

1. Assess for inguinal hernia.
2. Calculate TWIST score and refer the patient to the ED.
3. Order a urinalysis and urine culture.
4. Order a KUB radiograph to assess for kidney stones.

## TWIST Score

Testicular Workup for Ischemia and Suspected Torsion

- Helps establish or exclude testicular torsion
- TWIST score is higher in patients with torsion.
- $ Sensitivity 71%; Specificity 97%

| Test                      | Score                   |
|---------------------------|-------------------------|
| Testicular swelling       | 2 points                |
| Hard testis               | 2 points                |
| High-riding testis        | 1 point                 |
| Absent cremasteric reflex | 1 point                 |
| Nausea/vomiting           | 1 point                 |
| TOTAL                     | ≥5 concerns for torsion |

## Testicular Torsion

Twisting of testis and spermatic cord results in testicular ischemia if not corrected!

<!-- image -->

Joshua Lanclos/APEA

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #11

An 18-year-old patient has suspected testicular cancer. Which of the following characteristics is NOT associated with testicular cancer?

1. Unilateral swelling of one testis
2. Painless, firm nodule in the testis
3. History of cryptorchidism
4. History of hernia repair surgery

## Testicular Cancer

Males 15-35 years old

Hx of cryptorchidism (even with orchiopexy)

- $ Either testis affected
- $ Risk is greater in undescended one.
- Encourage testicular self-examination.
- Diagnostics
- $ Scrotal ultrasound
- Refer to Urology.
- $ Cryopreservation of sperm

## Other Scrotal Concerns

## VARICOCELE

- Swelling of VEINS
- "Bag of worms"
- May be painful or asymptomatic
- Can lead to low sperm count/quality or BPH

## HYDROCELE

- Fluid around testicle
- Common in infants-will resolve spontaneously
- If present in adults, may be benign or pathologic
- Transillumination

## QUESTION #12

A 44-year-old male has noticed mild discomfort in his left groin while exercising. There is a small "lump" in his groin that disappears when he lies supine. What is the diagnosis?

1. Ventral hernia
2. Umbilical hernia
3. Inguinal hernia
4. Incarcerated hernia

## Inguinal Hernias

- Two-thirds of inguinal hernias are on the right side.
- Inguinal hernias are the most common hernia type.
- Inguinal hernias are more common in males.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Joshua Lanclos/APEA

## QUESTION #13

A 20-year-old athlete has been diagnosed with an inguinal hernia. Which of the following should be recommended?

1. The athlete should be restricted from all athletic activity.
2. The patient should be referred to general surgeon.
3. The patient should be prescribed a truss.
4. Surgical repair should be deferred unless the hernia entrapped.

## Hernia Diagnosis

- Clinical diagnosis
- Ultrasound, if diagnosis is unclear

## Gynecomastia

Benign proliferation of glandular tissue of male breast

- Symptoms: asymptomatic or painful tender breast
- Differential diagnosis:
- $ Pseudogynecomastia
- Associated with obesity
- No well-defined rubbery mass
- $ Breast cancer
- Unilateral, nontender, hard, immobile mass, off-center from nipple

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #14

A late adolescent patient reports itching in the groin area. During the physical exam, the penis is notably <4.0 cm, and the testicles are smaller than expected. Scant pubic hair is present. Which action is most appropriate?

1. Advise the patient to follow up in 1 year.
2. Discuss measures for improving hygiene.
3. Refer the patient for evaluation of delayed puberty.
4. Ask the patient about previous sexual activity.
